newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore ends travel ban on ex-political prisoner.
newsitem.headline: Singapore ends travel ban on ex-political prisoner.

text.p: Singapore has lifted travel restrictions on an opposition politician more than 30 years after he was arrested under tough internal security laws and detained without trial.
A spokesman for the Ministry of Home Affairs told Reuters on Wednesday it had removed a travel ban on veteran socialist activist Chia Thye Poh and would allow him to leave the country.
Chia, now 56, had been a member of parliament for the opposition Barisan Sosialis party.

He was arrested on October 29, 1966 -- shortly after he and other Barisan members had resigned from parliament -- under the Internal Security Act (ISA), which allows detention without trial for renewable two-year periods.
He was never charged and remained in prison until May 1989, when he was allowed to live under restrictions on Sentosa, an island south of the city.
Since 1992 he has lived on the main island with his parents but his activities have remained heavily restricted.
A spokesman for the Ministry of Home Affairs confirmed Chia would continue to face certain restrictions, but declined to give details.
"We can confirm that travel restrictions have been lifted," he said, but added, "other restrictions still remain."
The ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has controlled Singapore's government since 1959, has said Chia was a communist and a threat to Singapore society.
Chia, who has become an icon for succeeding generations of opposition politicians, has always maintained his innocence.
He told Reuters on Wednesday he now wanted to leave Singapore, at least for a while, and take up an offer of a research post in public affairs and politics at the Hamburg Foundation in Germany.
"Now that I can travel, I am taking up an offer in the Hamburg foundation," Chia said in a telephone interview.
He said his health had deteriorated recently and he had problems with his prostate and also with his hearing.
"I will leave, if there is no urgent surgery needed, in end July or early August, for Germany," he said.
Chia said he still faced severe restrictions in Singapore.
"I cannot issue any public statements, attend public meetings, be a member of any associations or assist in their activities or be an adviser to any organisations.
"I cannot take part in political activities. I cannot communicate with ex-political detainees," he said.
"So now I am allowed to travel. But I am still not a free citizen in Singapore because of the remaining restrictions."
Asked if he was happy the travel restrictions had been removed, Chia said:
"It's 30 years since my arrest in 1966 so in fact all the conditions should have been lifted long ago. In the first place I should not have been arrested without trial."
